disease_name_ja: アルコール離脱せん妄

distillation_scope.scope_note: Full-spectrum first-layer disease manifold for delirium tremens/alcohol withdrawal delirium after chronic alcohol exposure and abrupt reduction or cessation. No case-specific evidence was used.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Long-standing alcohol exposure downregulates inhibitory GABA-A tone, upregulates glutamatergic NMDA signaling, and creates physiologic dependence. This is the background substrate that makes abrupt alcohol reduction capable of producing severe withdrawal delirium.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Abrupt alcohol reduction with GABA-NMDA rebound
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Acute drop in alcohol exposure unmasks low inhibitory GABA tone and excess NMDA-mediated excitability. This drives tremor, agitation, insomnia, seizures, and progression to delirium in susceptible patients.

Withdrawal excitability activates sympathetic output and hypothalamic stress signaling, producing tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, fever, nausea, tremor amplification, dehydration, and arrhythmia risk.

Global cortical and subcortical excitability with sleep deprivation and autonomic stress produces fluctuating attention, disorientation, agitation, visual/tactile/auditory hallucinations, and delirium tremens physiology.

Rapid shift toward excitatory neurotransmission lowers seizure threshold, especially in the first 6-48 hours after reduction, and is amplified by prior withdrawal seizures, electrolyte depletion, sleep deprivation, infection, or head injury.

Poor intake, vomiting, diaphoresis, osmotic losses, malnutrition, and catecholamine stress deplete water, magnesium, potassium, and phosphate. These abnormalities amplify delirium, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmias, and renal injury.

Alcohol use disorder commonly coexists with depleted thiamine and broader malnutrition. This does not define withdrawal itself but strongly modulates encephalopathy, Wernicke risk, electrolyte reserve, and treatment safety.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Complication cascade from severe withdrawal delirium
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe agitation, seizures, hyperthermia, dehydration, aspiration, sedative exposure, and comorbid liver/respiratory disease interact to produce respiratory failure, arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis, ICU-level care, and mortality hazard.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Alcohol withdrawal delirium requires a physiologic dependence substrate, usually after sustained heavy alcohol exposure.
The chronic alcohol substrate raises the scored harmful alcohol use context.
Physiologic dependence plus potential interruption raises withdrawal risk before overt delirium appears.
Abrupt reduction or cessation after dependence initiates the withdrawal rebound field.
The disease field is temporally anchored to hours since last substantial alcohol intake or abrupt dose reduction.
Excitatory rebound drives sympathetic activation.
Persistent excitatory rebound and sleep disruption progress from tremulous withdrawal to delirium.
GABA-NMDA rebound lowers seizure threshold early in withdrawal.
Sympathetic excess is directly expressed as autonomic hyperactivity.
Catecholamine excess produces sinus tachycardia and sometimes tachyarrhythmia.
Adrenergic output commonly raises blood pressure, though volume depletion can later blunt this.
Severe withdrawal can cause low to moderate fever through adrenergic thermogenesis and agitation.
Sweating is a direct autonomic withdrawal sign.
Tremor is a hallmark adrenergic and neuroexcitatory withdrawal sign.
Autonomic withdrawal can produce nausea and gastrointestinal upset.
Vomiting may occur from autonomic stress, gastritis, poor intake, or coexisting alcohol-related illness.
Delirium is expressed clinically as abnormal mental status with impaired attention and fluctuating cognition.
Alcohol withdrawal delirium requires delirium physiology rather than isolated uncomplicated tremulous withdrawal.
Fluctuating inattention distinguishes delirium from isolated anxiety or tremor.
Disorientation is a frequent cognitive expression of withdrawal delirium.
Alcohol withdrawal delirium commonly includes visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations.
Hyperactive delirium and agitation are common, though hypoactive or mixed delirium can occur in frail patients or after sedatives.
Insomnia and sleep fragmentation often precede and amplify withdrawal delirium.
Withdrawal seizure hazard is highest early and can coexist with or precede delirium.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are the usual clinical seizure phenotype in alcohol withdrawal.
Poor intake, diaphoresis, vomiting, and agitation deplete effective circulating volume.
Alcohol use disorder, poor intake, renal losses, and vomiting predispose to hypomagnesemia.
Vomiting, poor intake, catecholamine shifts, and concurrent hypomagnesemia promote hypokalemia.
Malnutrition and refeeding vulnerability can produce hypophosphatemia during withdrawal care.
Volume depletion can cause prerenal azotemia.
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, adrenergic stress, and QT-prolonging drugs can raise malignant arrhythmia hazard.
Poor nutritional reserve is common in severe alcohol use disorder and shapes withdrawal vulnerability.
Alcohol-related malnutrition raises thiamine deficiency context and Wernicke susceptibility.
Thiamine deficiency and carbohydrate exposure can precipitate or unmask Wernicke encephalopathy during withdrawal.
Delirium, vomiting, seizures, and sedative therapy raise aspiration risk.
Refractory agitation, oversedation, seizures, aspiration, or respiratory comorbidity can require airway control.
Severe agitation, restraint, hyperthermia, or seizures can cause rhabdomyolysis.
Mortality emerges from untreated severe delirium, seizures, aspiration, arrhythmia, dehydration, hyperthermia, respiratory failure, and comorbid organ disease.
The withdrawal delirium perceptual-disturbance network can produce hallucination/illusion activity as a severity satellite of abnormal mental status.
The withdrawal delirium perceptual-disturbance network can produce hallucination/illusion activity as a severity satellite of abnormal mental status.

axes.shape_free_text: Prior withdrawal delirium, withdrawal seizure, ICU-level withdrawal, or severe withdrawal requiring high sedative doses.
Autonomic hyperactivity cluster including tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, tremor, fever, nausea, vomiting, or adrenergic distress.

axes.display_name: 自律神経過活動の重症度
axes.shape_free_text: Severity of autonomic withdrawal signs across vital signs and physical findings.
Tachycardia attributable to withdrawal adrenergic tone after considering infection, pain, dehydration, arrhythmia, and medications.
Heart rate often rises during withdrawal delirium, but early, partially treated, volume-depleted, or sedated presentations can remain only mildly tachycardic.
Elevated blood pressure during withdrawal hyperadrenergic state; chronic hypertension may also contribute.
Blood pressure is commonly elevated during withdrawal delirium but can be normal or low with dehydration, sepsis, bleeding, oversedation, or early/partially treated disease.
Diastolic pressure may be elevated with adrenergic withdrawal tone, but normal values do not exclude withdrawal delirium.
Fever or hyperthermia history; withdrawal can cause low to moderate fever, while high or persistent fever should also raise competing infectious/toxic etiologies.
Measured body temperature.
Visible sweating or profuse diaphoresis during withdrawal.
Severity of sweating/diaphoresis.
Tremor, typically postural or action tremor, in the alcohol withdrawal syndrome.
Severity of tremor, including coarse tremor interfering with examination or function.
Any abnormal mental status such as confusion, delirium, reduced attention, agitation, psychosis, somnolence, or altered level of arousal.

axes.shape_free_text: Need for intubation or invasive mechanical ventilation because of refractory agitation management, respiratory failure, aspiration, seizure, or oversedation.

axes.display_name: アルコール離脱せん妄死亡ハザード
axes.shape_free_text: Disease-specific mortality hazard for alcohol withdrawal delirium, emerging from untreated severe delirium, seizures, aspiration, arrhythmia, dehydration, hyperthermia, respiratory failure, comorbid organ disease, and treatment toxicity.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Hallucination or psychotic perceptual disturbance severity during withdrawal delirium; visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations may occur as part of delirium tremens.
Visual hallucination or illusion severity during alcohol withdrawal delirium.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Recent reduction after dependence systematically raises withdrawal risk.
Autonomic withdrawal severity raises heart rate beyond baseline variability.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Hypertension effect can be blunted or reversed by dehydration, sepsis, bleeding, or oversedation.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Sympathetic tone raises blood pressure but competing volume/toxicity states can lower it.
Sweating, tremor, tachycardia, and hypertension fluctuate together with autonomic tone.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Hypoactive delirium, heavy sedation, frailty, or hepatic encephalopathy can reduce overt agitation despite severe mental status abnormality.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Alcohol withdrawal delirium is often hyperactive, but agitation is not obligatory in every patient.
Distressing hallucinations can amplify agitation and behavioral dysregulation.
Insomnia and circadian disruption increase delirium vulnerability and severity.
Low magnesium lowers seizure threshold and worsens potassium repletion.
Hypokalemia raises arrhythmia risk under catecholamine stress.
Severe hypophosphatemia can contribute to muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, and respiratory failure risk.
Seizures impair airway protection and can trigger aspiration.
Volume depletion increases prerenal AKI hazard.
Pigment nephropathy after rhabdomyolysis can cause acute kidney injury.
Thiamine deficiency is the substrate for Wernicke encephalopathy risk.
Oversedation or respiratory depression can require airway control and ventilation.
Aspiration pneumonia can progress to respiratory failure or sepsis and increases mortality hazard.
Malignant arrhythmia is a direct mortality pathway under catecholamine and electrolyte stress.
Airway failure and severe respiratory support needs mark high physiologic risk and treatment complexity.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe withdrawal delirium requires stronger control of the withdrawal field.
Sedative therapy can cause respiratory depression, especially with low airway reserve or co-intoxication.
Severe hepatic impairment favors shorter conjugated agents and closer monitoring; long-acting accumulation can worsen encephalopathy and respiratory depression.
effect_modifiers.treatment_modifier_ontology_note: Treatment modifier normalized as a scored hepatic impairment context.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Benzodiazepines restore GABAergic tone and reduce withdrawal excitability, autonomic stress, delirium, and seizure hazard; safety depends on respiratory and hepatic context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Phenobarbital can synergize with other sedatives and increase respiratory depression risk.
Liver disease and encephalopathy risk make barbiturate accumulation and oversedation more dangerous.
Phenobarbital provides strong antiseizure GABAergic control when withdrawal seizure hazard is high.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Phenobarbital extends GABAergic control and suppresses excitatory withdrawal physiology, but its long half-life and respiratory depressant effects require context-aware dosing and monitoring.

treatments.treatment_name: Propofol deep sedation for refractory withdrawal delirium

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Propofol-level sedation generally requires controlled airway and ventilatory support.
Deep sedation without airway control can worsen respiratory failure.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Propofol can control refractory agitation and excitability but reshapes the state through ICU sedation and airway management rather than treating the exposure substrate alone.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Alpha-2 agonism can reduce sympathetic signs but does not provide core GABAergic antiseizure control.
Dexmedetomidine can cause bradycardia and hypotension.
Hypotension limits alpha-2 agonist use.

autonomic_hyperactivity_severity.clinical_rationale: Reduces sympathetic variability and adrenergic surges.

agitation_severity.clinical_rationale: May reduce agitation variability while preserving arousability.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Dexmedetomidine modulates autonomic noise and agitation but should be represented as adjunctive physiology because it can mask symptoms without correcting GABA-NMDA withdrawal rebound.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Malnutrition increases thiamine depletion and Wernicke vulnerability.
Wernicke encephalopathy can overlap with withdrawal delirium and should be covered structurally rather than ignored.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Thiamine addresses a host vulnerability that overlaps clinically with withdrawal delirium and prevents carbohydrate-triggered Wernicke progression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal dysfunction changes potassium and magnesium replacement safety.
Malnutrition and refeeding increase phosphate depletion risk.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Electrolyte restoration reduces modifiable amplification of seizures, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, and weakness during withdrawal.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cirrhosis or hypoalbuminemia changes fluid tolerance and distribution.
Hypotension or volume depletion requires hemodynamic support and search for competing etiologies.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Volume repletion corrects dehydration-mediated tachycardia, renal stress, and electrolyte instability while avoiding sedation masking.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carbohydrate delivery without thiamine can worsen Wernicke risk.
Low phosphorus signals refeeding vulnerability.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Nutrition improves recovery reserve, but in alcohol withdrawal it must be coupled to thiamine and electrolyte surveillance.

treatments.treatment_name: Airway protection and mechanical ventilation support

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Airway control may be needed to safely deliver deep sedation for dangerous refractory withdrawal delirium.
Aspiration risk and respiratory failure hazard change airway and ICU support needs.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Airway protection is a supportive vector field that can lower death risk when respiratory failure or aspiration risk dominates, while also enabling deeper sedative control when needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Nonpharmacologic measures reduce noise but cannot alone suppress severe withdrawal excitability.

delirium_severity.clinical_rationale: Reduces environmental delirium fluctuation and nighttime worsening.

agitation_severity.clinical_rationale: Low stimulation, sitter monitoring, and reorientation can reduce behavioral volatility.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Environmental control and monitoring reduce delirium noise and injury/aspiration risk but do not replace withdrawal physiology control.

Observed harmful alcohol exposure directly raises the alcohol-use context axis.
Abrupt reduction is the core trigger of the withdrawal field.
Withdrawal risk rises sharply after abrupt reduction.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts GABA-NMDA rebound earlier and higher, with peak delirium commonly 48-96 hours after reduction.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Prior severe withdrawal indicates sensitized future withdrawal physiology.
Prior withdrawal seizure raises recurrent seizure risk.
Prior delirium tremens predicts severe withdrawal phenotype.
Frail or older patients have lower delirium reserve.
Poor reserve amplifies complications and treatment toxicity.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Frailty increases oversedation, fall, aspiration, and delirium persistence risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Physiologic stress amplifies sympathetic withdrawal expression.
Infection or trauma can raise fever independent of withdrawal and should remain a competing or comorbid field.
Acute illness raises complication and death risk.
Alcohol use disorder frequently coexists with chronic liver disease.
Hepatic impairment changes sedative metabolism and encephalopathy differential.
Liver disease increases infection, bleeding, encephalopathy, and sedative toxicity risk.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Long-acting sedatives may accumulate in liver disease.
Barbiturate accumulation and encephalopathy risk constrain use.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Malnutrition is the observed context.
Malnutrition raises thiamine deficiency risk.
Thiamine deficiency directly raises Wernicke hazard.

coupling_modulation.clinical_rationale: The thiamine-Wernicke pathway is stronger when nutritional reserve is poor.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Observed electrolyte depletion directly raises the electrolyte context.
Low magnesium, sodium abnormalities, and metabolic stress lower seizure threshold.
Low potassium and magnesium increase arrhythmia risk under adrenergic stress.
Respiratory compromise or sedative co-exposure directly raises treatment safety risk.
Low airway reserve amplifies sedative toxicity.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Respiratory compromise requires closer monitoring and may trigger airway support.
Barbiturate respiratory depression risk is higher with poor airway reserve.

supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Repeated structured assessment separates persistent withdrawal activity from oversedation, hepatic encephalopathy, infection, or other competing delirium fields.

supportive_care.care_name: Telemetry, vital sign, and airway monitoring
supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Severe withdrawal delirium can move quickly across autonomic, arrhythmic, and respiratory safety axes.
Electrolyte and renal axes change dynamically with vomiting, diaphoresis, refeeding, fluids, and renal function.
Withdrawal delirium creates preventable injury pathways through agitation, seizure, vomiting, impaired judgment, and sedation.

supportive_care.care_name: Evaluate competing causes of delirium and fever
supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Infection, head injury, hepatic encephalopathy, intoxication, hypoxia, metabolic disease, and intracranial pathology can coexist with or mimic withdrawal delirium; this is handled as differential/context evidence, not a disease-name qualifier.

supportive_care.care_name: Addiction medicine and relapse-prevention planning after stabilization
supportive_care.clinical_rationale: After acute delirium control, longer-term alcohol use disorder care changes future withdrawal risk and recurrent harm but is downstream of the acute SDE field.

notes: Mechanism-first distillation created from the pure disease name only: Alcohol withdrawal delirium.
No real case data, PubMed/PMC case details, or ranking failure information was used.

Alcoholic hallucinosis without delirium, uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal, hepatic encephalopathy, intoxication, sepsis, head injury, and primary psychosis are not encoded as exclusions; they should compete or superpose through their own manifolds/context axes.
Treatment effects are represented as vector-field reshaping, state pushes, sigma modulation, or theta modulation rather than semantic first-line labels.
